summary: Crypto lending and yield company that suspended customer inflows and outflows in October 2020, filed Chapter 11 in November 2020, and later became the subject of federal wire-fraud convictions involving former executives.
what_happened: Cred accepted cryptocurrency through CredEarn and offered crypto-backed borrowing through CredBorrow. Financial stress and undisclosed business problems preceded a late-October 2020 account halt and a 7 November 2020 Chapter 11 filing. A liquidation plan became effective on 19 April 2021. Former executives later pleaded guilty to wire-fraud conspiracy and were sentenced in August 2025. No reviewed source establishes one completed recovery percentage for every customer class.
uncertainty_notes: The 2018 launch date is approximate. Plan effectiveness is not repayment completion, and final recovery varies by claim class.
notes: Centralized crypto interest-account, bankruptcy and misconduct case.

summary: Crypto-backed lending platform that paused withdrawals in November 2022 after the FTX collapse affected its business, resolved a California licensing investigation through a 2024 borrower-refund settlement, and continued offering collateralized loans after license reinstatement.
what_happened: SALT offers loans secured by customer cryptocurrency. It paused withdrawals on 15 November 2022 and California suspended its lending license. A December 2024 consent order required borrower refunds, penalties, improved underwriting and disclosure practices, and procedures for closing or refinancing California loans. SALT states that its California license was reinstated effective 15 January 2025, and current first-party materials describe active loan and collateral-withdrawal functions.
uncertainty_notes: The 2016 launch date is year-level. Product availability and licensing vary by jurisdiction. The 2022 pause was not a company-wide bankruptcy.
notes: Active-survivor and regulatory comparator; the SALT token offering is tracked separately from borrower-collateral events.
